question: What are the construction characteristics of thee basic types of fuel tanks?
answer: The three types of tanks are rigid, bladder, and integral tank. The rigid tank is usually made of aluminum or stainless steel and is riveted and has welded seams to prevent leaks. Rigid tanks are removable. Some modern rigid tanks are made from composite materials. Bladder tanks are made from a reinforced flexible material. Bladder tanks are also removable. Bladder tanks are repairable by patching and other techniques in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. Integral tanks are formed as part of the wing or part of the fuselage and is sealed with a fuel resistant two part sealant to prevent leaks. A integral tank is not removable as it is part of the main structure of the aircraft. They are repairable by draining, cleaning, and resealing. All fuel tanks regardless of their construction must have means for venting, have a sump located at the lowest point where water and sediment can collect and be drained out. Many tanks have baffles to prevent the rapid movement of fuel during flight maneuvers and scuppers to drain away any spilled fuel at fill port areas.

question: What is the purpose of a fuel jettison system and what are some characteristics of a typical fuel jettison system?
answer: If an aircraft's design landing weight is less than that of maximum take off weight, a situation could occur in which a landing is desired before sufficient fuel has burned off to lighten the aircraft to or below the acceptable landing weight. Fuel jettisoning systems are required in these aircraft so that the fuel can be jettisoned in flight to avoid structural damage caused by landing the aircraft when it is to heavy. Characteristics of a fuel jettison systems are, the rate of fuel jettisoning as well as the various attitudes, speeds, and configurations of the aircraft are taken into consideration. The fuel must discharge clear of any part of the aircraft. The discharge of the fuel must not affect the controllability of the aircraft. There must be enough redundancy so that the failure of a single component does not prevent the fuel from being jettisoned. Also, the process of jettisoning fuel must be able to be controlled by a valve and stopped if desired. The amount of fuel able to be jettisoned is also controlled.

question: Explain the purpose and operation of a gyroscopic instrument.
answer: Most gyroscopic instruments are used for direction or attitude indication. They can be driven by air pressure, vacuum, or electricity since the spinning armature of a motor can act as a gyroscope. When rotating a gyroscope it maintains rigidity in space. That is, it will continue to rotate in the same plan of rotation no matter which way its mounting gimbals are moved. This is the basis of a directional gyro. The directional gyro, or DG is commonly relied upon more than the magnetic compass to indicate direction in an aircraft. The gyro spins in the vertical plane and stays aligned with the direction to which it is set. The instrument case and the aircraft move around the ridged gyro. This causes a vertical compass card geared to the rotor gimble to rotate. Typically, a small, fixed airplane in front of the moving card indicates the direction in degrees.

question: How does a pitot and static system operate?
answer: A pitot system captures air pressure as the aircraft moves forward through the air. Air travels through the pitot tube and the air pressure is converted to an airspeed indicator, and to the digital air date computer (if in use). The pressure is used to calculate and display airspeed. The static system is designed to sense ambient atmospheric pressure. Input air is either from static ports in the pitot tube, or from dedicated flush- mounted heated, static ports located on the side of the fuselage. The pressure is conveyed through a series of airtight tubes to the instruments that require the use of atmospheric pressure. This includes the air speed indicator, the variometer and the altimeter. On a modern more complex aircraft, the static system conveys ambient air pressure to a digital air data computer. In addition, the computer processes the ambient air pressure outputs for the auto-pilot system, the transponder, the flight management computers, IRS navigation units and more.

The cycle is than repeated (Vapor Cycle.) Components of the vapor cycle system are as follows: Evaporator, Compressor, condenser, receiver dryer, expansion valve. question: Briefly describe how an air cycle air conditioning system provides cool air to the aircraft cabin.
answer: Turbine engine bleed air is conditioned for use in the cabin during air cycle air conditioning. Turbine engine bleed air is let into the system where it then is routed to an air to air heat exchanger that cools bleed air with ambient ram air. The cooled bleed air is then directed into a compressor of the air cycle machine (ACM.) There it is compressed before flowing through a secondary air to air heat exchanger that again cools the air with ambient ram air. The bleed air flows back into the (ACM) where it drives an expansion turbine. This cools the air even further. Water is then removed via a water separator and the bleed air is then mixed with bypassed hot bleed air, and sent to the cabin at a temperature requested by the crew. Be prepared to discuss each component with the examiner. Each component of the air cycle machine(ACM) are as follows: Primary heat exchanger, secondary heat exchanger, compressor, expansion turbine, 35degree bypass valve, and a water separator.

question: Explain the two basic modes of cabin pressurization and name the single component that modulates to control the pressure of the air in the cabin during both modes of operation.

In isobaric mode, the pressurization system works to maintain a single pressure inside the cabin, known as cabin altitude, despite the altitude of the aircraft or the pressure of the ambient air outside the aircraft. In differential mode, the system controls the cabin pressure to maintain a constant pressure difference between the air inside the cabin and the air outside the aircraft regardless of altitude changes. The single device that opens and closes, or modulates to control air exiting the cabin, and thus, the air pressure in the cabin is the outflow valve.

question: What type of oxygen system is typically used on light, general aviation aircraft and what type(s) is used on transport category aircraft?
answer: Many light aircraft do not have an oxygen system if the aircraft is not designed to fly at altitudes that require oxygen. Some small general aviation aircraft may have a portable oxygen bottle on board to be used by the crew when desired. A built in system may exist that uses approved containers of gaseous oxygen. Both are typically delivered through regulated, continuous flow systems where oxygen is supplied at a steady rate when the valve of the oxygen container is opened. However, electronic pulse demand oxygen delivery systems are currently available for general aviation aircraft. These type pulse oxygen system only delivers oxygen to the user when they inhale creating a demand- type system. Oxygen is carried on transport category aircraft for emergency purposes only. During normal operation the cabin pressure provides enough oxygen for the crew and passengers. Gaseous and solid oxygen are used in an emergencies when pressurization is lost. The gaseous oxygen is stored in remote, pressurized tanks and routed to the users thorough a system of tubes. Solid oxygen generators produce gaseous oxygen for use when ignited. Passengers receive the oxygen from either source through a continuous flow delivery system. Most crew oxygen is delivered via demand flow or pressure- demand flow type regulators.

question: Name some precautions when performing maintenance on aircraft oxygen systems.
answer: Always keep clothing, hands, and tools clean, make sure there is no grease or oily residue around or near oxygen when servicing. A good maintenance practice is to have dedicated tools for servicing oxygen only. Never smoke or have an open flame within 50 feet of the work area when servicing oxygen. Always use protective plugs or caps when working with oxygen cylinders, system components or plumbing. Do not use any kind of adhesive tape. Oxygen cylinders should be stored in a designated, cool, ventilated area in the hanger away from petroleum products or heat sources. Fittings should be turned slowly to allow any residual pressure to dissipate. All oxygen lines should be marked and should have at least two inches of clearance from moving parts, electrical wiring, and all fluid lines. A pressure leak check must be performed each time the system is opened for maintenance. Do not use any lubricants, sealers, cleaners, etc., unless specifically approved for oxygen use.

question: What is the means of identification of commonly used communication and or navigation antennas?
answer: The shape and length of an antenna can sometimes be used to reason what type of antenna is under consideration. The orientation or polarization and location on the aircraft can also give clues. The three basic types of antennas are: the dipole, the Marconi, and the loop. Dipole antennas, often used for VOR frequencies, may have a “V” shape. They are commonly located at the empennage or mounted on the underside of the fuselage. The “V” shape indicates its horizontal polarization that makes the antennas good at receiving signals that are not coming head on. The Marconi antenna is simply a straight conductor. It uses the skin or on fabric aircraft, conductive material under the skin, to form a conductor of 2 wavelength of the signals it is designed to receive or transmit. The Marconi antenna is vertically polarized and creates a field that is omnidirectional. VHF communication radios can use this type of antenna. The conductor in a loop antenna forms a loop. Having a loop shape to receive radio signals significantly affects the field characteristics of the antenna. It is highly sensitive to the direction from which the signal is received. Loop antennas are used extensively in navigation such as for an ADF radio. Often the loop antennas are enclosed in a housing broad enough to conceal the entire antenna which is frequently mounted on the underside of the fuselage.

question: What are some common faults and trouble shooting techniques used on a fire detection system?
answer: Intermittent alarms most often are caused by loose wires can often be found by moving the wires to recreate the fault. Alarms and warnings of a fire when there is no fire present can be located by disconnecting the sensors from the control unit. If the alarm stops when the sensor is disconnected, the problem is the sensor. if all sensors are disconnected and the alarm continues, the problem is likely the control unit. Kinks and sharp bends in a sensing element can cause a short inside the sensing element. The fault can be located by checking the element with an ohm- meter while tapping the suspected areas to produce the short. Failure to obtain an alarm when a detection system is tested is often caused by a defective test switch or control unit, lack of electric power, inoperative indicator lamp or an opening in a sensing element or connecting wire. Check for power to test the circuit and replace the lamp. The continuity of a sensing loop can be determined by opening the loop and measure the resistance. Replacement of the test switch or control unit may be required if no other faults are discovered. Occasionally moisture can cause a false alarm. This is detected in a sensor loop when disconnected from the control unit. Replacement of the sensor solves the problem.

question: Describe how a Kidde and Fenwal continuous loop fire protection system functions.
answer: A Kidde system has a sensing element consisting of a sealed Inconel® tube containing two conductors that are embedded in a thermistor material. One wire is electrically grounded to the outer tube at each end and acts as an internal ground, and the other is a positive lead. When a fire or overheat occurs, the resistance of the thermistor material drops, allowing current to flow between the two wires to activate an alarm. A Fenwal system uses a sensing element consisting of a small diameter flexible Inconel tube containing a single wire electrode surrounded by ceramic beads. These ceramic beads prevent the electrode and tube from touching each other. Current is applied to the electrode while the outer tube is grounded to the aircraft structure. When a fire or overheat occurs, the core resistance of the ceramic beads drops, allowing current to flow between the center electrode and ground, energizing the alarm system.
